questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Slope as a constant rate of change
questions.learningObjective: interpret a slope as a constant rate of change along a straight line
questions.stem: A ramp climbs from street level to a raised loading dock, and at every stage of the climb the dock sits the same number of centimeters higher for each centimeter traveled forward. What does that repeated measurement say about the ramp?

options.text: Its rise over run is one fixed number, which is the ramp's slope
Its rise over run changes steadily as the climb continues upward
options.misconception: believes the rate of climb drifts as the ramp goes higher

options.text: Its rise over run is zero, since a steady climb adds no extra height
options.misconception: confuses a rising ramp with a level one and reports zero

options.text: Its rise over run equals its length, since height and distance are one
options.misconception: treats height gained as identical to distance traveled

questions.explanation: A slope is a ratio of two measured changes, rise over run, and on a straight line that ratio is the same no matter which piece of the line you measure it on. That constancy is exactly what makes the line straight: a curve would keep producing different ratios as you slide the measuring interval along it. The ratio may be any number at all, including zero for a level road, so a steady climb is a particular value of the ratio and not an absence of one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two measurements stay in the same proportion from one spot to the next.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Parallel lines and equal slopes
questions.learningObjective: state the slope condition for two nonvertical lines to be parallel
questions.stem: A drafting sheet shows two straight lines that will never meet anywhere on the paper, and neither of them is vertical. What must be true of the two lines for that to happen?

options.text: They have the same slope and are two genuinely different lines
They have opposite slopes that are equal in size but not sign
options.misconception: reads mirrored slopes as parallel rather than as a V shape

options.text: They have slopes whose product is negative one, as all lines do
options.misconception: borrows the perpendicularity rule and applies it to parallel lines

options.text: They have the same slope and pass through one common point
options.misconception: confuses two distinct parallel lines with a single line drawn twice

questions.explanation: Two nonvertical lines with the same slope rise by the same amount for every unit step sideways, so starting from any point on the first line, the second line at the same height lies the same horizontal distance away, and the gap never closes. The catch is the word different: lines with equal slope that share a point are one line described twice, not two parallel ones. Opposite equal slopes and negative reciprocal slopes describe lines that turn rather than lines that stay apart.
questions.hint: Think about the vertical gap between the two lines as you move to the right.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Perpendicular lines and negative reciprocals
questions.learningObjective: state the slope condition for two nonvertical lines to be perpendicular
questions.stem: Two straight lines on a grid cross each other at a right angle, and neither line runs straight up and down. How are their slopes related to one another?

options.text: They are negative reciprocals, so their product is negative one
They are equal, so the same rate of climb works in both directions
options.misconception: mistakes the perpendicular rule for the parallel rule about equal slopes

options.text: They are reciprocals, so their product is exactly positive one
options.misconception: drops the minus sign and keeps only the reciprocal part of the rule

options.text: They add to zero, so one climbs exactly as far as the other drops
options.misconception: confuses a product of negative one with a sum of zero

questions.explanation: A turn of 90 degrees rotates the direction of a line, and the new rate of climb is the old one tipped upside down, which both flips its sign and inverts it. Two lines at right angles therefore have slopes m and -1 over m, and their product is negative one, which also means a horizontal line can only be perpendicular to a vertical one. Equality, a product of positive one, and a sum of zero all describe pairs of lines that are not at right angles.
questions.hint: A quarter turn both flips the direction of travel and compresses the run.

questions.topic: Distance measured from horizontal and vertical offsets
questions.learningObjective: explain why the distance between two points combines the two offsets by a square root
questions.stem: Two markers sit on a gridded floor, one 8 squares to the right and 8 squares above the other. Why does the tape measure between them read longer than either offset alone?

options.text: The straight line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, so the square root is required
The straight line is longer than both offsets added together, since it bends
options.misconception: believes the diagonal can exceed the sum of the two legs it spans

options.text: The tape adds the two offsets and then doubles the result for the tape ends
options.misconception: invents an allowance for the width of the tape ends themselves

options.text: The straight line is the altitude of the right triangle, so it is the shorter leg
options.misconception: picks the shortest side of the right triangle instead of the hypotenuse

questions.explanation: Drop a vertical from the higher marker to the row of the lower one. The straight line can never beat the sum of the legs, it is the shortest of all routes, and it is certainly not the altitude.

options.misconception: adds the coordinates to get an endpoint rather than halving their sum

The closed curve made of every point whose distance to P and Q agrees
options.misconception: imagines a circle instead of the straight line of equidistant points

options.text: The two lines through P and through Q that both run parallel to PQ
options.misconception: places the stakes off to the side instead of along the crossing line

options.misconception: centres circles on the markers themselves and looks for a second fixed distance

questions.topic: Standard form of a line equation
questions.learningObjective: interpret the coefficients in the standard form of a line
questions.stem: A straight boundary is written as 3x plus 4y equals 12, with x and y measured in metres. What does that equation say about the boundary?

options.text: Every point on it has 3x plus 4y equal to 12, and it meets the axes at 4 and 3

options.text: Every point on it has 3x plus 4y at least 12, so the origin is outside
options.misconception: switches the inequality to the other side and moves the region with it

options.text: Every point on it satisfies 3x plus 4y exactly 0, since 12 adds no geometry
options.misconception: believes a nonzero constant in a line equation carries no information

questions.explanation: An equation in x and y of the first degree describes a single straight line, made of exactly those points that satisfy it, and the constant on the right is what places that line on the grid rather than through the origin. options.misconception: reads a coordinate difference as though it were a distance to the path

options.misconception: measures to an endpoint rather than to the nearest point on the path

A circle of centre (3, 4) and radius 25, the number on the right

options.misconception: swaps the two numbers naming the centre because both are subtracted

questions.topic: The three conic sections and their branches
questions.learningObjective: distinguish parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas by their equations
questions.stem: A set of points is described by the rule that x squared over 16 minus y squared over 9 always comes to one. What is the shape of that set?

options.text: A hyperbola, since the two squared terms subtract and the sign splits it in two
An ellipse, since both squared terms are divided and added in the rule
options.misconception: ignores the minus sign and reads the rule as a sum of two positive parts

options.text: A parabola, since one squared term and one plain term is all it takes
options.misconception: believes a rule needs a plain term rather than a second squared one

options.text: A circle, since any pair of squared terms can be rescaled to a round shape
options.misconception: assumes any equation in squares of coordinates must come out circular

questions.explanation: The sign between the two squared terms is what separates the conics. Added, they can describe a bounded closed oval, because the two stretches compete and the points run out of room. Subtracted, one term can grow faster than the other without bound, so the set falls into two pieces opening in opposite directions, which is a hyperbola. With one squared term and one plain term the set opens just once, and that is a parabola.

questions.topic: Why perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals

A quarter turn rotates that direction through 90 degrees, and rotation through 90 degrees in the plane sends a direction of one unit right and m units up to a direction of m units left and one unit up, because each part of the old direction is traded with the other and the sign of one of them changes. Since the new direction points one unit up for every m units right, its slope is the negative reciprocal, 1 over minus m, and multiplying gives m times negative one over m, which is negative one. The forcing fact is that a 90 degree turn maps one unit right to one unit up, so the two coordinates of the direction swap while one of them changes sign, and that swap is what produces the inversion.

Rotating a line through 90 degrees interchanges those two parts and reverses the sign of one of them, so a direction of one across and m up becomes a direction of m across with one down, which is a slope of negative one over m. Multiplying the two slopes then cancels m and leaves negative one, which is the whole content of the rule. The parallel rule is a different fact, since a line that is not turned keeps its ratio untouched rather than interchanging it.

questions.topic: Why a discriminant counts the crossings of a line and a circle

answer.exemplar: A line has one free parameter, its horizontal coordinate, so substituting it for one variable in the circle rule leaves a single quadratic equation in that one parameter, and the intersections of the line and the circle are exactly the solutions of that quadratic. A quadratic with real coefficients has two real roots when its discriminant is positive, one repeated root when the discriminant is zero, and no real roots at all when it is negative. The discriminant is the square of the difference of the two candidate roots, so a positive value means the two candidates are genuine and distinct points, a zero value means they have collapsed into a single point where the line is tangent, and a negative value means the two points are complex and the line never reaches the circle. That is why the three signs of the discriminant line up exactly with two crossings, one crossing, and no crossing.

The discriminant is a single number that decides that: it is a square, so it cannot be negative, its zero value collapses two equal roots into one tangent point, and its negative value means the roots are not real at all. Concentrating all of that information in one number is what makes the count readable without solving the quadratic.

questions.topic: Properties of a perpendicular bisector
questions.learningObjective: select the true properties of a perpendicular bisector
questions.stem: A segment joins two points P and Q, and its perpendicular bisector is drawn. Which of the following claims about that bisector are correct?

options.text: Every point on it lies at the same distance from P as from Q
It crosses segment PQ at a right angle rather than at a slant
It passes through the middle of segment PQ, which is the point of crossing
Every point of segment PQ itself is equally far from P as from Q
options.misconception: reads a statement about the bisector as though it described the segment

options.text: It is a closed curve centred on the middle of segment PQ
options.misconception: picture a closed curve rather than the straight line of equidistant points

questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector is defined as the locus of points equidistant from the two endpoints, so every point on it is as far from P as from Q, and the point where it crosses the segment is exactly the midpoint because a point on the segment is equidistant from the endpoints only at the middle. Its name also states the rest: it is perpendicular to the segment, and the crossing is a right angle. The claim about the whole segment is false because points near either end are much nearer that end, and a closed curve would have a bounded set of equidistant points when the set is in fact a whole line.
questions.hint: Ask what the word bisector names, and what the locus of equidistant points looks like.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Spotting conics from the sign between their terms
questions.learningObjective: classify conic equations by the signs of their squared terms
questions.stem: Five rules are printed on a screen, and the engineer needs to know which of them describe a hyperbola. Which rules are those?

options.text: x squared over 16 minus y squared over 9 equals 1, with the terms subtracted
y squared over 25 minus x squared over 4 equals 1, subtracted the other way up
x squared over 9 plus y squared over 16 equals 1, where the terms are added
options.misconception: ignores the plus sign and calls a bounded oval unbounded

options.text: x squared plus y squared equals 25, a single sum of two squared radii
options.misconception: treats any pair of squared coordinates as a two-branch curve

options.text: y equals 3x squared minus 4, with one squared and one plain term
options.misconception: expects two squared terms even when only one is squared at all

questions.explanation: A hyperbola is exactly the case where the two squared terms subtract, because then one can grow faster than the other without limit and the set falls into two branches. Both the first and the second rules have that subtraction, and swapping which variable is squared only turns the figure through a right angle, so both are hyperbolas. The third rule adds its squared terms and so is a bounded oval, the fourth is the special case where the two semi-axis lengths agree, and the fifth has a single squared term, which opens once and is a parabola.
questions.hint: Look only at the sign that joins the squared terms.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: What the distance between two points does and does not depend on
questions.learningObjective: identify the properties of the point-to-point distance formula
questions.stem: Two points on a grid are given, and the distance between them is wanted. Which of the following claims about that distance are correct?

options.text: It depends only on the two coordinate differences, not on where the points sit
It is never shorter than the larger of the two coordinate differences
It always equals the sum of the two coordinate differences and nothing else
options.misconception: believes a diagonal can be as long as the two legs added end to end

options.text: It is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the two differences
It is the average of the two coordinate differences taken together
options.misconception: divides by two on no basis, since nothing about the shape asks for a mean

questions.explanation: The formula combines the two coordinate differences and nothing else, so sliding both points by the same amount leaves the distance unchanged, which is the first claim. Because the straight line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with those two differences as legs, it is longer than either leg and so never shorter than the larger, which is the second claim, and that right-triangle reading is the third claim exactly. The sum is the route along the edges of the grid rather than the diagonal, and no averaging appears anywhere in the geometry.
questions.hint: Picture the right triangle whose legs are the two coordinate differences.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Area of a region drawn as a rectangle with a corner removed
questions.learningObjective: find the area of an L-shaped region from a drawn description
questions.stem: A workshop floor plan is drawn as a rectangle 12 metres by 7 metres, with a 5 metre by 3 metre rectangle cut out of the top right corner, leaving an L shape. What is the area of the L shape in square metres?

options.text: 69, from 84 square metres of rectangle less 15 cut away
69 is wrong and the area is 99, which adds the cut-out back on instead
options.misconception: adds the removed corner back instead of subtracting it from the whole

options.text: The floor covers 42, since a triangle's halving has been applied to a rectangle
options.misconception: applies a triangle's halving rule to a rectangle with no sides to spare

options.text: The floor covers 15, which is the area of the corner that was removed
options.misconception: reports the size of the removed piece as though it were the whole floor

questions.explanation: The whole rectangle covers 12 times 7, which is 84 square metres, and the corner that was cut away covers 5 times 3, which is 15. Removing it leaves 69 square metres, and the drawing is an L shape rather than a rectangle, so the two pieces have to be handled separately. Subtracting is the operation that matters: a notch taken out of a shape can only make the area smaller, and adding it back would describe a different floor entirely.
questions.hint: Find the area of the whole rectangle, then take away the area of the notch.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Chord length in a circle placed on a grid
questions.learningObjective: measure a chord in a circle whose equation is known
questions.stem: A round window is a circle with centre at (2, -1) and radius 6 on a grid, with all values in centimetres. Two points on its rim are marked at (2, 5) and at (8, -1). How long is the straight chord between those two marked points?

options.text: 8.49 cm, the hypotenuse over 6 right and 6 up from the centre
12 cm, which is the diameter of the window added to its radius
options.misconception: adds a radius to the diameter and calls the sum a single chord

options.text: 6 cm, which is the radius of the window used directly as the chord
options.misconception: takes a radius to be a chord whenever the chord happens to look long

options.text: 16.97 cm, which stretches the two offsets end to end
options.misconception: lays the two offsets end to end and calls the sum a straight line

questions.explanation: The first marked point sits 6 above the centre, so the second sits 6 to the right of it, and the chord between them runs 6 right and 6 down. That makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the chord, so the length is the square root of 36 plus 36, that is 8.49 centimetres. Both marked points are genuinely on the rim, since each is one radius from the centre, so the segment between them is a chord of the circle rather than something else entirely.
questions.hint: Each marked point is one radius from the centre, so use the centre to measure the offsets.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Crossing point of two lines read from a drawing
questions.learningObjective: find the intersection of two lines from their equations
questions.stem: A graph shows two straight roads drawn as the line y equals 2x plus 1 and the line y equals negative x plus 4, with distances in kilometres. At which point do the two roads cross one another?

options.text: (1, 3), where both rules give the same height at the same point
(2, 5), found by solving with the constant on the left dropped entirely
options.misconception: drops a constant from the equation and then solves a different one

options.text: (4, 9), found by reading a point off the first road and never checking
options.misconception: reads a value off one line and never checks the second line agrees

options.text: (0, 1), which is merely where the first road meets the vertical axis
options.misconception: takes an intercept of a single line and calls it a point where they meet

questions.explanation: At the crossing the two roads are at the same place, so their heights must be equal: 2x plus 1 equals negative x plus 4, which gives 3x equals 3, so x equals 1. Substituting back gives 2 times 1 plus 1, that is 3, so the crossing is at (1, 3), and the other line agrees since negative 1 plus 4 is 3. The crucial step is setting the two expressions equal, since that is what makes one point satisfy both rules at once.
questions.hint: At the crossing both rules give the same height, so set them equal.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Trapezoid read off a coordinate drawing
questions.learningObjective: measure the parallel sides and height of a trapezoid from coordinates
questions.stem: A garden bed is drawn on a grid with corners at (0, 0), (10, 0), (8, 5) and (2, 5), with all values in metres. What is the area of the bed in square metres?

options.text: 40, the mean of the bases 10 and 6 times the height of 5
50, which is the larger base multiplied by the height with no halving
options.misconception: uses one base alone and omits the halving the trapezoid requires

options.text: 80, which is the perimeter times the height over sixteen in error
options.misconception: mixes a perimeter measurement into a formula that takes two bases

options.text: 40, which treats both parallel sides as though each were 8 metres long
options.misconception: assumes the top edge is half the bottom edge without measuring it

questions.explanation: The bottom edge runs from (0, 0) to (10, 0), so it is 10 metres long, and the top edge runs from (2, 5) to (8, 5), so it is 6 metres long; the two are parallel because they are both horizontal. The height is the vertical gap between them, which is 5 metres. The area of a trapezoid is the mean of the parallel sides times the height, that is (10 plus 6) over 2 times 5, which is 40 square metres.
questions.hint: Measure both horizontal edges, then the vertical gap between them.

questions.topic: Graphing a line from slope-intercept form
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for graphing a line from slope-intercept form
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe graphing a straight line from an equation of the form y equals mx plus b. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Write down the constant b, which is where the line meets the vertical axis
Mark that point on the vertical axis of the empty grid, using its value
Move the stated slope across and up from that marked point, for one unit
Carry on repeating the same rise and run to sketch out the whole line

questions.explanation: The intercept is the only point on the line whose position the equation names outright, so it has to be read off and marked first, and it must be marked on the vertical axis because that is what the constant b means. Only once a real point exists can a direction be used to find a second one, and the slope is that direction, taken as the rise over the run. Sketching a line needs at least two points, and the repeating step extends them into a straight line rather than a pair of dots.
questions.hint: Nothing can be drawn until a point of the line is known.

questions.topic: Finding the distance from a point to a line
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of the point-to-line distance procedure
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe finding the distance from a point to a line written as Ax plus By equals C. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Substitute the coordinates of the point in place of x and y in the rule
Evaluate Ax plus By minus C at that point and take the size of the result
Square A and B, add them, and take the square root of that sum
Divide the size found earlier by the size of the coefficient pair

questions.explanation: The procedure is a formula, and a formula has to be fed in one piece at a time, so the coordinates go in first. Evaluating the leftover comes next, and taking its size at that moment is essential because the point may sit on either side of the line and a length has no sign. The size of the coefficient pair is a property of the line alone, independent of the point, so it can be found at any time, but it is needed before the division, which is the step that produces the answer.
questions.hint: Feed the point into the rule first, then do the arithmetic in a fixed order.

questions.topic: Rewriting a general circle rule in centre-radius form
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of completing the square in a circle equation
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe turning a rule with squared and linear terms into centre-radius form. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Group the terms by variable so that each variable's parts sit together
Complete the square for each variable, subtracting its compensation as you go
Move every compensation constant over to the right-hand side and add them up
Read the centre off the two brackets and take the square root for the radius

questions.explanation: The rewrite only works if the pieces of each variable are together, since a completed square needs the squared term and its own linear term in the same place, so grouping comes first. Completing each square then produces two brackets and two compensation constants, and those constants are what have to be gathered on the right, because that is where the single square number lives. Only once a lone number sits there can the two bracket values be read as the centre and its square root taken as the radius.
questions.hint: You cannot complete a square until its two terms are neighbours.

questions.topic: Area of a polygon from its listed vertices
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of the coordinate area procedure
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe finding the area of a quadrilateral from the coordinates of its four corners, listed around the boundary. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Write the corners in boundary order and repeat the first one at the end
Multiply each corner's x value by the next corner's y value, going round
Do the same multiplication with the roles of x and y reversed, going round
Take the size of the difference of the two totals and halve what remains

questions.explanation: The procedure walks around the boundary, so the corners have to be in boundary order and the walk has to be made closed by repeating the first corner, otherwise the last edge is left out. Two products are then taken around the loop, one in each direction, and only when both totals exist can they be compared. The difference between them is twice the area for a simple figure, so halving is the last step and is what turns a doubled figure into the true one.
questions.hint: The walk around the boundary must be closed before any totalling makes sense.

questions.topic: Showing a midpoint lies on a perpendicular bisector
questions.learningObjective: select the steps of a coordinate argument for a midpoint
questions.stem: Four labelled statements are offered for the task of showing, with coordinates, that the midpoint of a segment lies on that segment's perpendicular bisector. Which three of them actually belong?

options.text: Average the endpoints in each coordinate to get the midpoint of the segment
Measure the straight distance from that midpoint to each of the two endpoints
Multiply the two distances together to obtain the square of the whole segment
options.misconception: treats a product of two lengths as though it were a length itself

options.text: Observe that the two measured distances are equal, which is the defining property

questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector is defined as the set of points equidistant from the two endpoints, so the argument has to produce a point and then two equal measurements from it. Averaging gives the candidate point, measuring gives the two distances, and comparing them completes the proof. Multiplying the two distances serves no such purpose: a product of lengths is not a length, and the defining property is an equality of two lengths rather than any single number made from both.
questions.hint: The definition is about two lengths being equal, so build two lengths and compare them.

questions.topic: What must be checked before two lines are called parallel
questions.learningObjective: select the necessary checks in a parallelism test
questions.stem: Four labelled statements are offered for the task of deciding, from their equations, whether two straight lines are parallel. Which three of them actually belong?

options.text: Rewrite each line with one variable alone on its own side of the rule
Compare the two slopes that this rewriting makes visible, looking for equality
Confirm that the two intercepts differ, so the lines are distinct ones
Confirm that the two intercepts agree, which would make one line only
options.misconception: believes matching intercepts prove parallel rather than coincident lines

questions.explanation: Slopes are only comparable once each line has been rearranged so that one variable stands alone, so that step has to come first, and the equality of the two slopes is the substantive test. A separate check is then needed, because equal slopes alone are not enough: if the intercepts also agree, the two equations describe the same single line, and a line is not parallel to itself. Requiring the intercepts to differ rules out that case and leaves two genuinely separate lines that never meet.
questions.hint: Equal slopes can describe one line described twice, so something must rule that out.

questions.topic: Fitting a circle through three surveyed points

questions.stem: Four labelled statements are offered for the task of finding the circle through three points that have been surveyed. Which three of them actually belong?

options.text: Take the midline of the side joining the first two of the three points
Take the midline of another side, and find where the two midlines cross
Measure from that crossing point to one of the points to get the radius
Draw a circle through the origin centred on the point that was surveyed first
options.misconception: centres on a surveyed point and forces the circle through an unrelated origin

questions.explanation: A circle's centre is equally far from every point on the circle, so it must lie on the midline of any chord, and two different chords give two different midlines whose crossing is forced. The radius then follows from the centre to any one of the three points, and all three give the same length, which is the natural check that the fitting has worked. Centring on a surveyed point and forcing the circle through the origin serves neither purpose and would generally miss all three points.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof that a computed midpoint is equidistant
questions.learningObjective: prove a midpoint is equidistant from the endpoints using coordinates
questions.stem: Write a short proof that the point whose coordinates are the averages of those of (a, b) and (c, d) is the same distance from each of those two points.

answer.exemplar: Let M be the point ((a + c) / 2, (b + d) / 2), and let P = (a, b) and Q = (c, d). The distance from M to P is the square root of (((a + c) / 2 - a)^2 + ((b + d) / 2 - b)^2). Since (a + c) / 2 - a = (c - a) / 2 and (b + d) / 2 - b = (d - b) / 2, that distance is the square root of ((c - a)^2 + (d - b)^2) / 4. The distance from M to Q works out the same way, because (a + c) / 2 - c = (a - c) / 2 and (b + d) / 2 - d = (b - d) / 2, whose squares are the same two numbers, so that distance is also the square root of ((c - a)^2 + (d - b)^2) / 4. The two are therefore equal, and since a point equally far from two fixed points lies on their perpendicular bisector, M lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: The proof works by reducing both measurements to the same pair of squares. Each half-sum minus an endpoint is one half of a difference, and squaring removes the sign, so both distances reduce to a quarter of the same sum of squares. Equality of the two is then automatic rather than coincidental, and the definition of the perpendicular bisector converts that equality into the geometric conclusion.
questions.hint: Reduce each half-sum minus an endpoint to half a difference before squaring.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof of the distance formula
questions.learningObjective: derive the distance formula from the Pythagorean theorem
questions.stem: Write a short proof that the distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is the square root of the sum of the squares of their two coordinate differences.

answer.exemplar: Take P = (x1, y1) and Q = (x2, y2), and drop a vertical from P to the point R = (x2, y1). Since PR is vertical and RQ is horizontal, the angle at R is a right angle, and the segment PQ is the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose legs are PR and RQ. Those legs are PR = |x2 - x1| and RQ = |y2 - y1|, because PR is the horizontal gap between the two x values and RQ is the vertical gap between the two y values. By the Pythagorean theorem, PQ squared equals PR squared plus RQ squared, which is (x2 - x1) squared plus (y2 - y1) squared. Since a length is not negative, taking the positive square root gives PQ = the square root of ((x2 - x1) squared + (y2 - y1) squared), which is the required formula. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: The only way to apply the Pythagorean theorem is to exhibit a right triangle with the segment as its hypotenuse, and dropping a vertical from one endpoint does exactly that. The two legs then turn out to be the horizontal and vertical gaps, with no other content to compute. Squaring is what allows the signs to disappear, and the final square root is forced because a distance is a length and lengths are not negative.
questions.hint: Complete the figure into a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the segment itself.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof that a diameter determines a circle's equation
questions.learningObjective: prove that a given diameter fixes the centre-radius form of a circle
questions.stem: Write a short proof that a circle whose diameter has endpoints (a, b) and (c, d) has centre at their midpoint and radius equal to half their distance apart.

answer.exemplar: Let P = (a, b) and Q = (c, d) be the endpoints of the diameter, and let M = ((a + c) / 2, (b + d) / 2) be their midpoint. A diameter is by definition a chord that passes through the centre, and the centre of a circle is the point halfway between the two ends of any diameter, because those two ends are one radius away in opposite directions. Hence the centre is M. The radius is half the diameter, so it is half the distance from P to Q, that is the square root of ((c - a) squared + (d - b) squared) all divided by 2. A circle is the set of points at that radius from its centre, so in centre-radius form its equation is (x - (a + c)/2) squared + (y - (b + d)/2) squared = ((c - a) squared + (d - b) squared) / 4. Both the centre and the radius have been produced from the two endpoints alone, and either endpoint satisfies the equation because substituting it returns exactly the squared radius. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: Two separate facts do the work here. The first is that a diameter is a chord through the centre, so its midpoint is the centre and its half-length is the radius. The second is that the midpoint formula already gives that midpoint in coordinates, and the distance formula already gives the length of the diameter. Substituting both into the centre-radius form of a circle produces the equation directly, which is why a diameter is often the most convenient pair of data to be handed.
questions.hint: A diameter is a chord that passes through the centre, so its midpoint is the centre.
